SpectralFM — label regression eval

Does the embedding beat raw input?

A frozen SSL backbone embeds each 245-point radio-telescope spectrum into a 768-dim vector. This page asks the practical question: for regressing a scalar label, does that embedding beat just using the raw 245 numbers — and specifically, does it beat raw input in the few-shot regime a foundation-model probe would actually operate in?

00

Overview

Label: parameter_0, the labeled_data subset (n=4,716 usable spectra, 12 unique components — 2 exact duplicates dropped). Backbone: the frozen SSL data2vec-audio checkpoint. Every number on this page passed a shuffled-label canary — refitting the identical pipeline on randomly permuted labels collapses it to ≈0, confirming nothing here is a measurement artifact.

The embedding side of this comparison was searched hard — four phases, over every block, five pooling schemes, and ten probes — specifically so a "raw input wins" verdict couldn't be blamed on an under-tuned embedding recipe.

how uncertainty is reported

No number here is a bare point estimate. Three uncertainties appear; they answer different questions and are never conflated.

SymbolWhat it isAnswers
± split SDSD across 3 repeated shuffled 5-fold splitsDoes recipe A really beat B on this data?
± bootstrap SDSD of R² under resampling of the 4,716 spectraWould this survive a different sample?
[IQR]25th–75th percentile across repeated training drawsHow much does which rows you label matter?

Draws per ladder rung: 100 at ntrain≤50, 40 at 100–200, 15 at 500, 6 at 1,000, 3 at 2,000, 1 at the full pool — there is only one way to take every row, so that point carries a bootstrap SD instead of an IQR.

02

Method

Raw-input baselines — three, all checked

Raw input's 245 features are highly collinear (adjacent spectral bins carry almost the same information). A standard shrinkage probe (RidgeCV) applies uniform shrinkage across all directions — which washes out signal living specifically in the thin, near-degenerate directions collinearity creates. Whitening (PCA-whitening, fit label-free on the unlabeled corpus) fixes this directly by decorrelating the feature space before the probe ever sees it.

PLS solves the same problem a different way: it looks at features and labels together and constructs a few new axes explicitly chosen to correlate with the label, no longer collinear with each other. Ordinary regression on those few axes then recovers signal RidgeCV alone never could — not because the regression got smarter, but because the hard geometric problem was already solved by the projection before regression saw the data. This is real and large at full sample size (PLS-64 and whitening land at comparable raw-input ceilings, 0.824 vs. 0.833 at 1-component). Whitening is used as the primary baseline here because it's unsupervised — free of any risk of a supervised- projection leak — and simpler to apply consistently across every sample size in the ladder below. Plain z-scoring is included too, as the "did nothing clever" floor.

Embedding recipe — searched, not assumed

Four phases, each narrowing from the last.

1

Which block

Mean-pooled, both normalizers, across all 15 blocks (FE ×2, Projector, Transformer layer 1–12). Full ranking in the scoreboard below.

2

Which pooling scheme

Tried only on the phase-1 winner: mean, mean+std, mean/max/min, four-segment (the FE's 47 output tokens split into 4 contiguous chunks, pooled separately), first+last token.

3

Concatenation

Does combining the top-2 blocks from phase 1 beat the single best block alone?

4

Which probe

Tried only on the phase 1–3 winner: RidgeCV, PLS at 4 ranks, PCA+Ridge at 3 ranks, gradient boosting, k-NN.

Protocol: RidgeCV, 5-fold CV (unless phase 4 says otherwise for the embedding). Label-efficiency ladder at n_train ∈ {10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,716}, repeated random draws per rung (100 draws at n≤50, down to a single draw at the full pool), reporting the median.

scope note

The 4-phase search ran once, at 1-component, full pool. The winning recipe is reused unchanged at 2- and 3-components — it was not independently re-optimized per component count. The 2–3-component embedding numbers below are a lower bound on what a per-component search might find, not a fully independent optimum.

⚠ the top three are a statistical tie

Transformer layer 2 leads the Projector by 0.004 — smaller than the Projector's own split SD (±0.008). This is not hypothetical: an earlier single-split pass of this same search ranked the Projector first and Transformer layer 2 second. The ranking flipped between runs because the difference is noise.

The defensible claim is "the Projector and Transformer layers 1–2 are the strongest taps, and are indistinguishable from each other" — not that any one of them is the best block.

What is well separated: the top group beats Transformer layer 3 (0.826 ±0.002) by far more than either SD; signal then decays monotonically with depth; and the conventional final-layer tap (0.674 ±0.011) is the weakest Transformer-side option. The two FE taps are both weakest and least stable — FE (post-LN)'s ±0.087 is an order of magnitude noisier than any Transformer tap.

Squeezing the winning block further

All at 1 component, ntrain=4,716; ± is the split SD.

  • Pooling (on Transformer layer 2, standardized): four-segment 0.909 ±0.003 beats mean+std 0.868 ±0.012, first+last 0.867 ±0.007 and plain mean 0.853 ±0.001. The +0.056 gain over plain mean is far outside both SDs — the single largest gain the embedding search produced.
  • Concatenation (Transformer layer 2 + Projector, mean-pooled): 0.849 ±0.019 vs 0.853 ±0.001 for layer 2 alone. No gain — the two blocks carry redundant, not complementary, signal, consistent with their being statistically tied.
  • Probe (on layer 2 / segment4 / standardized): plain RidgeCV 0.909 ±0.003 beat all nine alternatives, nearest PLS-64 at 0.836 ±0.002. That 0.073 margin is decisive: on the embedding side, dimensionality reduction costs signal — the opposite of the raw-input side.

winning embedding recipe

Transformer layer 2, four-segment pooling, standardized, plain RidgeCV — 0.909 ±0.003 (1 component, ntrain=4,716). The Projector and Transformer layer 1 are tied with layer 2 as the underlying block.

05

Does the gap ever close?

ComponentsCrossing point95% bootstrap CIGap at ntrain=4,716
1n ≈ 1,027[965 – 2,380]+0.079

⚠ the crossing point is poorly determined

The CI spans 965 to 2,380 — a factor of 2.5. The honest statement is "somewhere around one to two thousand labels", not a precise figure. An earlier pass of this analysis reported n≈1,191 from a single unbootstrapped estimate; that precision was not real.

What is solid: at 1 component the gap does cross and stays positive; at 2 and 3 components it never crosses at any ntrain tested. The dip between ntrain = 20 and 100 is a real feature, not noise — raw input's advantage is widest exactly in the regime a few-shot probe would operate in.

True vs. predicted

08

Leak check

Every configuration in every table above was refit on randomly permuted labels. Real R² stays large and positive; shuffled R² lands between −0.059 and −0.001 across all 15 checks (3 component counts × 5 recipes), confirming none of these numbers are measurement artifacts.

09

What this means

the embedding's real win

At 1 component with the full 4,716-spectrum pool the embedding genuinely wins — 0.912 ±0.010 against 0.833 ±0.004 for whitened raw input, a margin several times the uncertainty on either side. The crossing happens somewhere around ntrain ≈ 1,000–2,400.

but not where it matters most

At 2 and 3 components, raw input wins at every ntrain tested including the full pool, by margins well outside the error bars (0.937 ±0.002 vs 0.897 ±0.004, and 0.964 ±0.001 vs 0.906 ±0.004).

In the few-shot regime (ntrain ≤ 500), whitened raw input leads at every component count including 1 — and by the reliability measure (fraction of draws beating the mean) the gap is starker still. The embedding's win only materialises once labeled data is plentiful, which is the opposite of few-shot.

For the stated goal — a few-shot regressor over the embedding as a foundation-model probe — the conclusion survives a deliberately hard search on the embedding side: raw input remains the stronger substrate wherever labels are scarce.

a methodological finding worth carrying forward

The block ranking was not stable across runs until uncertainties were added. A single 5-fold pass picked a different "best block" than three repeated passes did, purely from split noise. Any future block or checkpoint comparison on this task should report repeated-split SDs before declaring a winner.

10

Recommendations

1

Use the embedding at 1 component with ≥ ~2,000 labels

Transformer layer 2 (or the Projector, or Transformer layer 1 — they are tied), four-segment pooled, standardized, plain RidgeCV. Above the crossing CI's upper bound the win is unambiguous.

2

Use whitened raw input everywhere else

All of ntrain ≤ 500 at any component count, and 2–3 components at any ntrain. Whitening is label-free and consistently the strongest raw-input recipe.

3

Do not use the conventional final-layer tap

At 0.674 ±0.011 (1 component, ntrain=4,716) Transformer layer 12 is the weakest Transformer block and 0.24 below the best recipe.

4

Report repeated-split uncertainty in any future comparison

The ranking flip above shows single-split point estimates are not sufficient to choose between nearby recipes.

5

Still untested

Stratified or active label selection (every draw here was i.i.d. random), per-component-count recipe search, other checkpoints (notably reconstruction-trained ones), and distribution shift / calibration — this study is entirely in-distribution.

11

Reproducing this

cd code
/mnt5/noy/miniconda3/envs/spectralfm_env/bin/python3 -m eval.label_probe \
  --checkpoint /mnt5/noy/SpectralFM/checkpoints/runai/runai_long_train_2026-02-25_13-46-46.pt \
  --data /mnt5/noy/SpectralFM/fairseq/data/nova_data/labeled_data \
  --out_dir eval_outputs/label_probe/<run_name> \
  --device cuda --comps 1 2 3

Redraw every figure from a finished run's JSON — seconds, no checkpoint or GPU:

python3 -m eval.label_probe --plots_only \
  eval_outputs/label_probe/<run_name>/label_probe_results.json

The embedding-feature bank (bank.npz, several GB) is cached in out_dir and reused on a rerun with the same path — delete it to force re-extraction. Embedding extraction is a single forward pass over the full dataset (a few minutes); the 4-phase recipe search plus the label-efficiency ladders across all three component counts take several hours, dominated by repeated RidgeCV fits at the smaller sample sizes and by the phase-1 scoreboard (15 blocks × 2 normalizers, at full-pool n).

Code: code/eval/label_probe/ — fairseq-free, tested (pytest eval/label_probe/tests/ --import-mode=importlib from code/).
